faq.a: To detect unexpected antibodies that could cause hemolysis, ensuring compatible donor blood and patient safety.
faq.q: Why is antibody screening done before every transfusion?

faq.a: No; antibodies may not have formed yet. Repeat the screen 2‑3 days after the transfusion.
faq.q: Can a negative screen be trusted in a patient who was transfused yesterday?

faq.a: Use washed red cells, consider plasma‑reduced components, or arrange for donor recruitment; monitor closely for hemolysis.
faq.q: What if the identified antibody is rare and antigen‑negative units are unavailable?

ai.title: Antibody Screening in Transfusion Medicine
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Antibody screening detects clinically significant red cell antibodies to prevent hemolytic transfusion reactions. It guides safe blood selection, especially where resources are limited.

b: Uses patient serum + reagent red cells
Detects IgG antibodies that can cause delayed hemolysis
First step before cross‑match
sections.p: Antibody screening is a laboratory test performed on a patient’s serum to identify unexpected antibodies against red blood cell antigens. It is done before any transfusion or during pregnancy to avoid hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN).

b: Screening cells express the most common antigens (K, Jk^a, S, etc.)
A negative screen means no clinically significant antibodies detected
A positive screen mandates an antibody identification panel
sections.p: The test relies on the indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) reaction. Positive results require identification of the specific antibody and selection of compatible donor units.

b: Pregnant women: prevents HDFN
Patients with sickle cell disease or thalassaemia: frequent transfusions increase alloimmunisation risk
HIV/TB patients: may need multiple transfusions; screening avoids added complications
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, transfusion‑related hemolysis is a major cause of morbidity. Proper antibody screening reduces mortality and conserves scarce blood supplies.
When IAT reagents are unavailable, perform a manual tube test using pooled donor cells and anti‑IgG. If no lab, rely on thorough transfusion history and avoid antigen‑positive units.

t.b: Does the patient have any unexpected red cell antibodies? – Positive: proceed to antibody identification; Negative: safe to cross‑match with standard units
Which specific antibody is present? – Determines compatible donor phenotype; if unavailable, use antigen‑negative blood or washed cells
Is there antibody bound to the patient’s own red cells? – Positive DAT suggests autoimmune hemolysis or recent transfusion reaction

b: Select antigen‑negative donor units based on identified antibody
If specific antigen‑negative units unavailable, consider washed red cells or plasma‑reduced components
Document antibodies in the patient’s record for future transfusions
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause of antibody formation and ensure compatible transfusion. Monitor for delayed hemolysis after transfusion.

b: IAT = screening for antibodies in serum
DAT = testing patient’s red cells for bound antibody
sections.p: Direct Coombs test (DAT) which detects antibodies already attached to the patient’s red cells, not circulating antibodies.

b: Cold agglutinins may give false‑positive IAT at room temperature – keep samples at 37 °C
Autoantibodies can mask underlying alloantibodies – perform adsorption studies if clinically indicated
sections.p: Low‑titer antibodies may be missed; weak reactions can be false‑negative if incubation time is insufficient.

b: Positive IAT → antibody ID → antigen‑negative units
IgG antibodies cause delayed hemolysis; IgM cause immediate hemolysis (rare in screening)
In emergencies, give O‑negative blood after rapid screen if life‑threatening
sections.p: Focus on the steps after a positive screen, the significance of IgG vs IgM antibodies, and transfusion strategies when compatible blood is scarce.

b: Assuming a negative screen rules out all antibodies – repeat after 2‑3 weeks if recent transfusion
Failing to document antibodies – leads to repeat alloimmunisation
Using pooled cells without known antigen profile – may miss rare antibodies
sections.p: Misinterpreting a negative screen as no risk, ignoring patient history, and using antigen‑positive units in allo‑immunised patients.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute hemolysis after transfusion (dark urine, jaundice, hypotension)
Severe anemia with rapid drop in hemoglobin post‑transfusion
Unexplained fever and rigors during or after transfusion
